subject: Physiology
summary: Spermatogenesis is the 74‑day production of sperm in seminiferous tubules, driven by Sertoli‑cell support and Leydig‑cell testosterone. Clinicians assess it when evaluating infertility, endocrine disorders, or testicular toxicity.

sections.p: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. It is a continuous, 74‑day cycle that transforms spermatogonia into mature spermatozoa, requiring tight coordination between germ cells, Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
b: Spermatogonia (stem cells) → primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids → spermatozoa

sections.p: The process has two main phases: spermatocytogenesis (proliferation and meiosis) and spermiogenesis (maturation). Sertoli cells provide nutrients, physical support, and a blood‑testis barrier, while Leydig cells secrete testosterone that fuels the entire cycle.
b: Sertoli cells form the blood‑testis barrier, secrete lactate and androgen‑binding protein

t.b: Detects structural lesions or tumors that may impair spermatogenesis; abnormal echotexture suggests damage
High FSH indicates Sertoli cell dysfunction or germ cell loss; low FSH with normal testosterone suggests primary testicular failure
Low LH with low testosterone points to central hypogonadism; normal LH with low testosterone suggests Leydig cell failure

sections.p: Hypothalamic GnRH pulses stimulate pituitary LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to produce testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support germ cell development. Testosterone feeds back negatively on GnRH and LH.
b: GnRH pulse frequency: high pulses favor FSH, low pulses favor LH

sections.p: Disruptions can arise from genetic defects, infections, toxins, or endocrine disorders. Common causes in low‑resource settings include HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis, and herbal remedies containing gonadotoxins.
b: Genetic: Klinefelter, Y‑chromosome microdeletions, CFTR mutations

t.b: Assesses sperm count, motility, morphology; abnormal results guide further endocrine or genetic testing
Low testosterone with normal FSH suggests Leydig cell failure; high testosterone with low sperm count may indicate endocrine resistance

sections.p: Clinicians evaluate spermatogenesis in infertility workups, endocrine disorders, and when assessing testicular toxicity from drugs or environmental exposures.

t.b: Differentiates primary testicular failure from secondary hypogonadism

sections.p: Remember the 74‑day cycle and the two phases. High FSH with normal testosterone indicates primary testicular failure. Low testosterone with normal FSH suggests central hypogonadism.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe testicular pain, swelling, or signs of infection (e.g., epididymitis)
Rapid decline in semen quality with unexplained endocrine changes

faq.q: What is the normal sperm count?
faq.a: At least 15 million sperm per milliliter with 40% motility and 4% normal morphology.
Yes, many herbs contain compounds that inhibit Leydig cells or damage germ cells, leading to reduced sperm production.

faq.q: How long does it take for testosterone therapy to restore sperm?
faq.a: Sperm production may resume after 3–4 months of adequate testosterone levels, but recovery depends on underlying cause.

exam: Explain the hormonal regulation of spermatogenesis and the roles of FSH and LH.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a man with non‑obstructive azoospermia.
Outline the management of testicular toxicity caused by a commonly used antimalarial drug.
